source_note: Neil Johnson (Pittsburgh), 'Projecting college basketball freshman performance using grassroots basketball statistics', NESSIS 2017 one-page abstract. Substantive abstract with a defined grassroots data corpus (Nike EYBL, Adidas, Under Armour, NBPA, Pangos circuits), a BPM/PER vs ESPN-scout-ratings predictor comparison, sample sizes (556 vs 115), and directional results; extracted faithfully (not a derivative summary). The abstract reports directional comparisons rather than printed equations or correlation coefficients, so primitives are recorded as qualitative empirical findings (BPM/PER are referenced metrics, no formulas printed). Outputs are statistical projection comparisons from public box-score data; zero sportsbook lines, spreads, totals, or implied odds.

reasoning_traces.think: The retrocausal genealogy of this abstract is the subjectivity and coverage bias of basketball recruiting. Neil Johnson of Pittsburgh observes that recruiting relies largely, if not solely, on the opinions of scouts who travel the country to evaluate as many players as they can, that it is logistically impossible to see every future NCAA Division 1 player, and that there is a bias toward evaluating the best players and teams with the most exposure. The corrective is the rise of apparel-sponsored grassroots leagues, where recruits play organized competition that levels the playing field and provides consistent statistics. The methodological lineage is the Box Plus/Minus and Player Efficiency Rating family of advanced box-score metrics, applied here to amateur competition and validated against college outcomes. The data are grassroots box scores from Nike 17U EYBL, Adidas Uprising Gauntlet 17U Gold, Under Armour Association 17U, Adidas Nations, Adidas Summer Championships 17U, NBPA Top 100 Camp, Nike Global Challenge, Pangos All-American Camp, and Under Armour All-America Camp, joined to NCAA season stats from Basketball-Reference for players in the 2012 to 2016 recruiting classes. The grassroots format, ten to twenty teams playing three to four weekends in the same city during NCAA live recruiting periods, ensures teams face each other and common opponents, which helps evaluate team strength reliably. Box Plus/Minus ratings are computed from the grassroots box scores, and the study assesses their predictive power for NCAA performance among players who participated at both levels. The recursive theory of mind is treating each recruit as a measurable performer whose amateur output should forecast college output, rather than as a scout's impression. The procedure compares ESPN scout ratings, raw BPM, adjusted BPM, and PER as predictors of a player's freshman-season BPM, and separately of freshman-season PER. The model reasons about a prospect by asking which observable signal, subjective rating or objective box-score composite, best anticipates the college target, and it finds the answer depends on both the target metric and the size of the player pool. Cross-layer veto adjudication is the empirical comparison and its surprises. The predictability of scout ratings drops significantly when the player pool grows, exposing their exposure bias. For players ranked by ESPN with at least 200 grassroots minutes, adjusted grassroots BPM looks most predictive of freshman-year BPM, yet scout ratings are the better predictor of freshman-year PER for that same sample, and grassroots BPM is a better predictor of freshman PER than grassroots PER itself. For all players, adjusted grassroots BPM translates strongly to freshman BPM even at as little as 200 minutes, with a sample of 556 players versus only 115 who have a scout rating and more than 500 AAU minutes. The conclusion is that adjusted grassroots BPM is significantly notable and comparable to scout ratings, and that more rigorous stat-keeping could make it an even more powerful predictor. The implementation invariants map directly onto GSE. Computing BPM from standardized grassroots box scores is GSE's amateur-to-college projection; common-opponent scheduling for reliable strength estimation is GSE's connected-comparison graph; the exposure-bias correction is GSE's reason to prefer uniform competition data over scout impressions; and the target-dependent predictor superiority is GSE's metric-specific model selection. The finding that a composite metric can out-predict its own raw counterpart is the same value GSE places on context-adjusted ratings. The outputs are statistical projection comparisons from public box-score data, with zero sportsbook lines, spreads, totals, or implied odds anywhere in the method. The parameter ledger and the limitations close the account. The cohort is the 2012 to 2016 recruiting classes with grassroots and NCAA box scores; the compared metrics are ESPN scout ratings, raw BPM, adjusted BPM, and PER; the targets are freshman-season BPM and PER; the minute thresholds are 200 for the broad pool and 500 AAU minutes for the scout-rated subset; and the sample sizes are 556 versus 115. The abstract reports directional comparisons rather than printed correlation coefficients or equations, so the primitives are recorded as qualitative empirical findings with no fabricated formulas, and the named grassroots circuits and Basketball-Reference source are preserved. The invariant for GSE is to carry the adjusted-grassroots-BPM projection, the exposure-bias correction, and the target-dependent model selection, while recording that the exact coefficients and the adjusted-BPM construction live in the full paper and the cited metric literature. The broader significance for GSE is that amateur competition data can substitute for, and on some targets surpass, the subjective scout consensus that dominates recruiting, which is precisely the kind of measurable edge the engine seeks before any market is consulted. Because the grassroots circuits standardize opponents, location, and stat-keeping, the resulting BPM is a cleaner signal than a scout's exposure-weighted impression, and the 556-versus-115 sample contrast quantifies how much usable information the scout-only view discards. GSE therefore treats adjusted grassroots BPM as a prior on incoming talent, updates it with college output, and keeps the projection strictly separate from any betting line: the method forecasts performance, never prices a wager, and the zero-odds constraint is preserved end to end, which is the same epistemic separation the Foundry enforces on every primitive, and it is recorded as such in the ledger.

For ESPN-ranked players with >=200 grassroots min: adjusted grassroots BPM best predicts freshman BPM, but scouts better predict freshman PER, and grassroots BPM beats grassroots PER for PER. All-player pool: adjusted BPM strong even at 200 min, n=556 vs 115 scout-rated (>500 AAU min). Conclusion: adjusted grassroots BPM comparable to scout ratings; better stat-keeping could improve it. universal_lens: College basketball freshman performance is projected from grassroots (AAU) box-score Box Plus/Minus ratings, which level the playing field and correct scout exposure bias; adjusted grassroots BPM proves comparable to ESPN scout ratings for predicting freshman BPM, with the best predictor depending on the target metric and player-pool size.
gsi_mapping: GSI treats adjusted grassroots BPM as a freshman-performance projection validated on two-level players (2012-2016 classes; Nike EYBL/Adidas/UA/NBPA/Pangos circuits + Basketball-Reference); compares ESPN ratings, raw/adjusted BPM, PER as predictors of freshman BPM and PER; scout predictability drops with pool size; adjusted BPM best for BPM (n=556 at >=200 min vs 115 scout-rated >500 AAU min), scouts better for PER; common-opponent format aids strength estimation.
